result.summary: Pausanias tells how Hera, angry with Zeus, was tricked by Cithæron into a sham wedding with a wooden statue, and so was reconciled. He then describes the festivals of the Dædala, small and great, held by the Platæans and all Bœotia, with their oak-image making and great bonfire on Cithæron.

scenes.title: Cithæron's trick on Hera
scenes.summary: Zeus, unable to appease Hera, follows Cithæron's advice and parades a dressed wooden statue as a bride. Hera tears its clothes, laughs, and is reconciled.
scenes.stakes: Zeus risks losing Hera's favour and his marriage.

scenes.title: Origin of the name Dædala
scenes.summary: Pausanias reasons that statues were called dædala before Dædalus the Athenian, who got his name from his statues. He notes uncertainty about the festival's interval.

scenes.title: The oak-coppice and crows
scenes.summary: The Platæans put out boiled meat in an oak grove near Alalcomenæ and carve the image from the tree where a crow perches. The great Dædala is held every sixth year for all Bœotia.

scenes.title: The great procession and bonfire
scenes.summary: Bœotian towns draw lots for statues, take them by waggon from the Asopus to Cithæron and burn them with sacrifices on a great wooden altar. A cave of the prophetic Nymphs lies below.

notable_quotes.reason: The comic climax: Hera finds a wooden bride and is delighted by the trick.

analysis.text: The passage gives a playful myth as the origin of a ritual, explaining how a divine quarrel and reconciliation became a festival.
The festival shows Bœotian unity and politics: the towns joined the Platæans after Cassander restored Thebes.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias admits he could not learn the exact interval between festivals even though he tried.

language_notes.text: Dædala is plural of Greek daidalon, meaning a carved or ornamented work, here a wooden statue; the word also underlies the name Dædalus.
Pausanias argues the craftsman took his name from the statues, not the reverse: 'from his statues, and not from his birth' means his name was not given at birth.
'Antiquarian guide' is a local expounder of antiquities who showed Pausanias the sights; the term is the translator's rendering.
The Asopus is the river near Platæa; a stade is about 185 metres.
Sphragidion means roughly 'little seal'; the name belongs to the cave of the prophetic Nymphs on Cithæron.

context_notes.text: Cithæron is here a mythical king of Platæa, also the name of the mountain near Thebes and Platæa, sacred to Hera and Zeus.
Cassander, son of Antipater, ruled Macedonia and refounded Thebes in 316 BC after Alexander had destroyed it; Thebes had been hostile to Platæa.
Burning victims whole, with wine and incense, was a holocaust-style offering; Hera and Zeus were the divine married pair honoured here.

literary_notes.text: The mighty king of gods is reduced to deceiving his wife with a doll, a comic reversal of divine dignity.
The quick, linked clauses of 'and... and...' mimic the swift reversal of Hera's rage into laughter and reconciliation.
The flame is 'prodigious' and visible from an immense distance, conveying awe at the festival's grandeur.
